title: Naming Livery Stable Blues and the Max Hart copyright
summary: He explains how the tune was named at Victor and that agent Max Hart copyrighted it in his own name.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Now what about the Aeolian Vocalian records? Who did you use? Well, I'll tell you. Was that late before that one went off?
That brings in another story. I better tell that story before I go too far. And will that be ahead of London?
No. Be ahead of a story, wouldn't it?

Yeah, this should come before London. After the first Victor release called Liberty Stable Blues, When we went to record this number to Victor, we were told the name was suggested. And to change the name by our blues. We went over and had this thing taken down. And Max Hart, who was the theatrical agent, had this number. Instead he copyrighted on my name like it should have been. He copyrighted on his own name and he was the only to copyright. This man, had we just been a flash in the pan, this man would have been a millionaire today. So, this is the case of the Liberty Stable Blues. Nunes, who had played with me, said he helped to compose the tour. Or it would have been who gave me the name, the original name, because I had no name for none of my tunes. I'd call them Dirt, Snot Ball, anything else. Just like that. Each one, they'd play some of your Dirt. They'd say to me, play some Dirt. Well, that's what I'd play, understand? Some of these make up tunes that I had. They had no name to them.
